results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets within 10 of the LAST-shown example (and not within 10 of the first) minus on targets within 10 of the FIRST-shown example (and not within 10 of the last); observed != null (model is order-invariant, so null ~ stimulus-driven difference) means example order matters: > null = recency, < null = primacy.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: For sets of >=2 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets within 10 of the LAST-shown example (and not within 10 of the first) minus on targets within 10 of the FIRST-shown example (and not within 10 of the last); observed != null (model is order-invariant, so null ~ stimulus-driven difference) means example order matters: > null = recency, < null = primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(s)
    arrs = [np.array([int(x) for x in u.split(",")]) for u in uniq]
    first = np.array([a[0] for a in arrs])[codes]
    last = np.array([a[-1] for a in arrs])[codes]
    n = np.array([len(a) for a in arrs])[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ins = np.array([str(tt) in u.split(",") for tt, u in zip(t, s)])
    nl = np.abs(t - last) <= 10
    nf = np.abs(t - first) <= 10
    base = (n >= 2) & ~ins
    a = base & nl & ~nf
    b = base & nf & ~nl
    ra = y[a].mean() if a.any() else 0.0
    rb = y[b].mean() if b.any() else 0.0
    return float(ra - rb)

results.name: cell_unanimity_fraction
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells with >=4 responses in which all responses agree (all yes or all no); observed > null means people's answers are more deterministic/consensual per item than the model's graded posterior probabilities imply (model too uncertain), observed < null means people are more heterogeneous.

results.name: small_minus_large_target_rule_consistent
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all even, yes-rate on even non-example targets <=50 minus on even targets >50; observed > null means people favour small numbers within an endorsed rule (a magnitude bias) beyond what the model's examples-driven intervals produce, observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: small_minus_large_target_rule_consistent
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all even, yes-rate on even non-example targets <=50 minus on even targets >50; observed > null means people favour small numbers within an endorsed rule (a magnitude bias) beyond what the model's examples-driven intervals produce, observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(s)
    arrs = [np.array([int(x) for x in u.split(",")]) for u in uniq]
    ok = np.array([len(a) >= 2 and bool(np.all(a % 2 == 0)) for a in arrs])[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ins = np.array([str(tt) in u.split(",") for tt, u in zip(t, s)])
    m = ok & ~ins & (t % 2 == 0)
    a = m & (t <= 50)
    b = m & (t > 50)
    ra = y[a].mean() if a.any() else 0.0
    rb = y[b].mean() if b.any() else 0.0
    return float(ra - rb)

results.name: even_sets_even_target_inrange_minus_outrange
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all even, yes-rate on even non-example targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus on even targets outside it; observed > null means people combine the parity rule with a range restriction ("even numbers around these") more than the model, whose even/multiples rules ignore magnitude.
results.code:
# name: even_sets_even_target_inrange_minus_outrange
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all even, yes-rate on even non-example targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus on even targets outside it; observed > null means people combine the parity rule with a range restriction ("even numbers around these") more than the model, whose even/multiples rules ignore magnitude.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    arrs = [np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq]
    ok = np.array([len(a) >= 2 and bool(np.all(a % 2 == 0)) for a in arrs])
    lo = np.array([a.min() for a in arrs])[codes]
    hi = np.array([a.max() for a in arrs])[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ins = np.array([str(tt) in s.split(",") for tt, s in zip(t, df["number_set"].astype(str))])
    m = ok[codes] & (t % 2 == 0) & ~ins
    a = m & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    b = m & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    ra = y[a].mean() if a.any() else 0.0
    rb = y[b].mean() if b.any() else 0.0
    return float(ra - rb)

results.name: outlier_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate when the target is itself one of the shown examples AND the other >=3 examples all share a parity or a last digit that this example lacks (an odd-one-out example, e.g. 100 in 31,19,49,100); observed < null means people discard odd-one-out examples as noise more than the model, which nearly always keeps every example inside the concept.

results.name: set_level_yes_rate_dispersion
results.description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=20 responses) of each set's overall yes-rate; observed > null means people's overall willingness to generalize differs between sets more than the model predicts (model too homogeneous across sets, e.g. too broad for tight sets or too narrow for loose ones), observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: set_level_yes_rate_dispersion
# description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=20 responses) of each set's overall yes-rate; observed > null means people's overall willingness to generalize differs between sets more than the model predicts (model too homogeneous across sets, e.g. too broad for tight sets or too narrow for loose ones), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df["rating"].astype(float).groupby(df["number_set"].astype(str)).agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 20]
    return float(g["mean"].std(ddof=0)) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: odd_mult3_sets_oddnon3_minus_evenmult3
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples that are all odd multiples of 3, yes-rate on odd non-multiples of 3 minus yes-rate on even multiples of 3; observed > null means people generalize such sets by oddness more (and by "multiples of 3" less) than the model, which lacks the conjunctive "odd multiples of 3" concept and over-weights multiples of 3.
results.code:
# name: odd_mult3_sets_oddnon3_minus_evenmult3
# description: For sets of >=3 examples that are all odd multiples of 3, yes-rate on odd non-multiples of 3 minus yes-rate on even multiples of 3; observed > null means people generalize such sets by oddness more (and by "multiples of 3" less) than the model, which lacks the conjunctive "odd multiples of 3" concept and over-weights multiples of 3.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    ok = np.array([(lambda a: len(a) >= 3 and bool(np.all(a % 2 == 1)) and bool(np.all(a % 3 == 0)))(np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")])) for s in uniq])
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = ok[codes]
    a = m & (t % 2 == 1) & (t % 3 != 0)
    b = m & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 3 == 0)
    ra = y[a].mean() if a.any() else 0.0
    rb = y[b].mean() if b.any() else 0.0
    return float(ra - rb)

results.name: rule_conflict_majority_rule_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples whose examples do NOT all share a parity, yes-rate on non-example targets having the parity shared by all but one example (e.g. odd targets for 31,19,49,100); observed > null means people generalize by the majority rule, tolerating one exception, more than the model, which falls back to intervals when no rule covers every example.
results.code:
# name: rule_conflict_majority_rule_yes_rate
# description: For sets of >=3 examples whose examples do NOT all share a parity, yes-rate on non-example targets having the parity shared by all but one example (e.g. odd targets for 31,19,49,100); observed > null means people generalize by the majority rule, tolerating one exception, more than the model, which falls back to intervals when no rule covers every example.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(s)
    arrs = [np.array([int(x) for x in u.split(",")]) for u in uniq]
    maj = np.full(len(arrs), -1)
    for i, a in enumerate(arrs):
        if len(a) >= 3:
            odd = int((a % 2).sum())
            if odd == len(a) - 1:
                maj[i] = 1
            elif odd == 1:
                maj[i] = 0
    mp = maj[codes]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ins = np.array([str(tt) in u.split(",") for tt, u in zip(t, s)])
    m = (mp >= 0) & ~ins & (t % 2 == mp)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
